title: CDNs and HTTP caching
subtitle: A CDN answers from a copy near the user. Your HTTP headers decide what it may copy, for how long, and for whom.

c.v: Early on 25 December 2015 (Pacific time), the Steam Store was under a denial-of-service attack. Traffic to the store rose by 2,000% over the average during the Steam Sale.

To reduce the load on its store servers, Valve deployed caching rules managed by a web caching partner. During a second wave of the attack, a second caching setting was deployed. In Valve's words, it "incorrectly cached web traffic for
So pages built for logged-in users were cached and returned to other users. Between 11:50 and 13:20 PST, store page requests for about 34,000 users may have been shown to someone else.

Those pages could contain a billing address, the last four digits of a Steam Guard phone number, purchase history, the last two digits of a card number, or an email address. Full card numbers and passwords were not exposed.
Valve shut down the store and deployed a new caching setting. The store stayed down until all caching settings were checked and cached data was purged from the
Valve called it a configuration error. The
did what its settings said, and the settings were wrong. This lesson is about writing those settings well.
(content delivery network) keeps copies of your content in data centers that are closer to users than your own servers. This makes pages faster and takes load off your servers.
The data centers near users are called edge locations. Your own server, which has the real content, is the
An edge location is a shared cache: it stores responses and reuses them for more than one user. A browser cache is a private cache: it serves one user only.
The CDN must answer two questions for each response:
May I store this, and for how long?
Which later requests may get this copy?
A CDN is only as safe as your headers and your cache key. If two different users can produce the same cache key, they can see each other's pages.

The cache key decides which requests share one stored copy. In the standard, it is at least the request method and the URL.

Sometimes one URL can return different versions, chosen by the request headers. The

A cache may reuse a copy without checking the origin only if those request headers match.

Changing content: purge or a new name
When content changes, you have two choices.
You tell the CDN to drop copies. Cloudflare can purge one URL, a prefix, a tag, a hostname or everything. It recommends purging single URLs.

Fastly has URL, surrogate key and purge-all options. A soft purge marks a copy stale, so it can still be served while a new one is fetched. A hard purge removes it, so the next request goes to the origin. Purge-all is always hard.

The HTML is checked on each load, and it points to the new names.
Two more directives help when a copy goes stale. With
, a cache may serve the stale copy for a short time. Meanwhile it fetches a fresh one in the background. With
, it may serve the stale copy when the origin returns a 500, 502, 503 or 504 error.
Both come from a separate standard, RFC 5861, not from RFC 9111.
At a CDN, many users may miss on the same URL at once. Fastly's request collapsing sends only one of them to the origin, and the rest share the answer.
A CDN has many edge locations. Each one that misses goes to your origin. A shield adds one more layer. Edges ask a chosen shield location, and only the shield asks the origin.
Cloudflare's Tiered Cache works the same way, with lower tiers and upper tiers.

This reduces origin requests. The cost: traffic between Fastly locations counts toward your bill. Also, a request that reaches the origin counts as two misses, so your reported hit ratio can look lower than you expect.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: response, on purpose. Do not leave the choice to CDN defaults.
"Is this response the same for every user?"
When you add CDN rules, test them with two different logged-in users. Check that user B never sees user A's data.
Review CDN config changes like code. The Steam leak came from a cache setting deployed in a hurry.
Fastly's 2021 outage came from a valid customer config change that hit a hidden bug. About 85% of its network returned errors.
Track the cache hit ratio and origin requests per second. A sudden drop often means a new query string or header split the cache key.
Avoid purge-all in busy hours. At Fastly, purge-all is a hard purge, so every object must be fetched from the origin again.
Know your plan B. If the CDN fails, can your origin carry the full traffic?
"List every HTTP endpoint in this service and the Cache-Control header it sends. Mark any response that depends on the logged-in user but is not private or no-store."
"Change our build so JS and CSS files get a content hash in the name. Serve them with max-age=31536000, immutable, and serve index.html with no-cache."
"Write a test that logs in as two users, requests /account through the CDN, and fails if the second user sees the first user's email."
No response with personal data can be stored in a shared cache. Look for
or user IDs to the cache key "to be safe". That splits the cache into one copy per user.
Hashed file names change when the content changes, and only then.
The CDN config change is reviewed, and you know how to roll it back.
